mushroom. Following his death, many sources have attributed it to his being fed a meal of death caps instead of
Caesar's mushrooms. Ancient authors, such as <color=#3366CC>Tacitus</color> and <color=#3366CC>Suetonius</color>, are unanimous about poison having been
added to the mushroom dish, rather than the dish having been prepared from poisonous mushrooms. Wasson
speculated the poison used to kill Claudius was derived from death caps, with a fatal dose of an unknown poison
(possibly a variety of <color=#3366CC>nightshade</color>) being administered later during his illness. Other historians have speculated that
Claudius may have died of natural causes.
In the 2023 Leongatha mushroom murders, Australian woman Erin Patterson was found guilty of three murders and
one attempted murder of members of her estranged husband's family by serving them beef Wellingtons that contained
A. phalloides. Three of the four guests died within days of the meal, while one survived after weeks in a coma.
Australia (continent)
The <color=#3366CC>continent</color> of Australia, sometimes known in technical contexts as Sahul, Australia-New Guinea, Australinea, or
Meganesia to distinguish it from the <color=#3366CC>country of Australia</color>, is located within the <color=#3366CC>Southern</color> and <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> hemispheres, near
the Maritime Southeast Asia. The continent includes mainland Australia, <color=#3366CC>Tasmania</color>, the island of <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color> (<color=#3366CC>Papua</color>

<color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color> and <color=#3366CC>Western New Guinea</color>), the <color=#3366CC>Aru Islands</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Ashmore and Cartier Islands</color>, most of the <color=#3366CC>Coral Sea</color>
<color=#3366CC>Islands</color>, and some other nearby islands. Situated in the geographical region of <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color>, more specifically in the
subregion of <color=#3366CC>Australasia</color>, Australia is the <color=#3366CC>smallest of the seven traditional continents</color>.
The continent includes a <color=#3366CC>continental shelf</color> overlain by shallow seas which divide it into several landmasses—the
<color=#3366CC>Arafura Sea</color> and <color=#3366CC>Torres Strait</color> between mainland Australia and New Guinea, and <color=#3366CC>Bass Strait</color> between mainland
Australia and Tasmania. When <color=#3366CC>sea levels</color> were lower during the <color=#3366CC>Pleistocene ice age</color>, including the <color=#3366CC>Last Glacial</color>
<color=#3366CC>Maximum</color> about 18,000 BC, they were connected by dry land into the combined landmass of Sahul. The name "Sahul"
derives from the Sahul Shelf, which is a part of the continental shelf of the Australian continent. During the past 18,000
to 10,000 years, rising sea levels overflowed the lowlands and separated the continent into today's low-lying arid to
<color=#3366CC>semi-arid</color> mainland and the two mountainous islands of New Guinea and Tasmania. With a total land area of 8.56
e6km2, the Australian continent is the smallest, lowest, flattest, and second-driest continent (after <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>) on <color=#3366CC>Earth</color>.
As the country of Australia is mostly on a single landmass, and comprises most of the continent, it is sometimes
informally referred to as an island continent, surrounded by oceans.
Papua New Guinea, a country within the continent, is one of the most culturally and linguistically diverse countries in
the world. It is also one of the most rural, as only 18 percent of its people live in urban centres. <color=#3366CC>West Papua</color>, a region in
Indonesia, is home to an estimated 44 uncontacted tribal groups. Australia, the largest landmass in the continent, is
highly <color=#3366CC>urbanised</color>, and has the world's 12th-largest economy with the among the highest human development index
globally.
Terminology
The continent of Australia is sometimes known by the names Sahul, Australinea, or Meganesia to differentiate it from
the country of Australia, and consists of the landmasses which sit on Australia's continental plate. This includes

mainland Australia, <color=#3366CC>Tasmania</color>, and the island of <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color>, which comprises <color=#3366CC>Papua New Guinea</color> and <color=#3366CC>Western New</color>
<color=#3366CC>Guinea</color> (Papua and West Papua, provinces of <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>). The name "Sahul" takes its name from the Sahul Shelf,
which is part of the continental shelf of the Australian continent. The term <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color>, originally a "great division" of the
world in the 1810s, was replaced in <color=#3366CC>English language</color> countries by the concept of Australia as one of the world's
continents in the 1950s.
Prior to the 1950s, before the popularization of the theory of <color=#3366CC>plate tectonics</color>, <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>, Australia and <color=#3366CC>Greenland</color> were
sometimes described as island continents, but none were usually taught as one of the world's continents in
English-speaking countries. Scottish <color=#3366CC>cartographer</color> John Bartholomew wrote in 1873 that, "the <color=#3366CC>New World</color> consists of
<color=#3366CC>North America</color>, and the peninsula of <color=#3366CC>South America</color> attached to it. These divisions [are] generally themselves spoken
as continents, and to them has been added another, embracing the large island of Australia and numerous others in
the [Pacific] Ocean, under the name of Oceania. There are thus six great divisions of the earth — <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>,
North America, South America and Oceania."
The American author Samuel Griswold Goodrich wrote in his 1854 book History of All Nations that, "geographers have
agreed to consider the island world of the Pacific Ocean as a third continent, under the name Oceania." In this book the
other two continents were categorized as being the New World (consisting of North America and South America) and
the <color=#3366CC>Old World</color> (consisting of Africa, Asia and Europe). In his 1879 book Australasia, British naturalist <color=#3366CC>Alfred Russel</color>
<color=#3366CC>Wallace</color> commented that, "Oceania is the word often used by continental geographers to describe the great world of
islands we are now entering upon" and that "Australia forms its central and most important feature." He did not explicitly
label Oceania a continent in the book, but did note that it was one of the six major divisions of the world. He considered
it to encompass the insular Pacific area between Asia and the Americas, and claimed it extended up to the <color=#3366CC>Aleutian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Islands</color>, which are among the northernmost islands in the Pacific Ocean. However, definitions of Oceania varied during
the 19th century. In the 19th century, many geographers divided up Oceania into mostly racially-based subdivisions;

<color=#3366CC>Australasia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Malaysia (encompassing Malay Archipelago)</color>, <color=#3366CC>Melanesia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Micronesia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Polynesia</color>.
Today, the Malay Archipelago is typically considered part of <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, and the term <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color> is often used to
denote the region encompassing the Australian continent, <color=#3366CC>Zealandia</color>, and various islands in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color> that are
not included in the <color=#3366CC>seven-continent</color> model. It has been recognized by the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> as one of the world's five

major continental divisions since its foundation in 1947, along with <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>. The UN's
definition of Oceania utilizes four of the five subregions from the 19th century; Australasia, Melanesia, Micronesia, and

Polynesia. They include <color=#3366CC>American Samoa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Australia</color> and their external territories, the <color=#3366CC>Cook Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Easter Island</color>

(<color=#3366CC>Chile</color>), the <color=#3366CC>Federated States of Micronesia</color>, <color=#3366CC>French Polynesia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Fiji</color>, <color=#3366CC>Galapagos Islands</color> (<color=#3366CC>Ecuador</color>), <color=#3366CC>Guam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kiribati</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Marshall Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nauru</color>, <color=#3366CC>New Caledonia</color>, <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color>, <color=#3366CC>Niue</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Northern Mariana Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ogasawara</color> (<color=#3366CC>Japan</color>),

<color=#3366CC>Palau</color>, <color=#3366CC>Papua New Guinea</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pitcairn Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Samoa</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Solomon Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tokelau</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tonga</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tuvalu</color>, <color=#3366CC>Vanuatu</color>, <color=#3366CC>Wallis</color>

<color=#3366CC>and Futuna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Western New Guinea</color>, and the United States Minor Outlying Islands (<color=#3366CC>Baker Island</color>, <color=#3366CC>Howland Island</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jarvis</color>

<color=#3366CC>Island</color>, <color=#3366CC>Midway Atoll</color>, Palmyra Atoll, and <color=#3366CC>Wake Island</color>) as well as <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color> (one of 50 states of the United States). The
original UN definition of Oceania from 1947 included these same countries and semi-independent territories, which
were mostly still <color=#3366CC>colonies</color> at that point.

The island states of <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>, <color=#3366CC>Singapore</color> and <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color>, all located within the bounds of the
Pacific or associated marginal seas, are excluded from the UN definition. The states of <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color> and <color=#3366CC>Malaysia</color>,
located in both mainland Asia and marginal seas of the Pacific, are also excluded, as is the nation of <color=#3366CC>Brunei</color>, which
shares the island of <color=#3366CC>Borneo</color> with Indonesia and Malaysia. Further excluded are <color=#3366CC>East Timor</color> and <color=#3366CC>Indonesian (or</color>
<color=#3366CC>Western) New Guinea</color>, areas which are biogeographically or geologically associated with the Australian landmass. This
definition of Oceania is used in statistical reports, by the <color=#3366CC>International Olympic Committee</color>, and by many atlases. The
CIA World Factbook also categorize Oceania or the Pacific area as one of the world's major continental divisions, but
use the term "Australia and Oceania" to refer to the area. Their definition does not include Australia's subantarctic
external territory <color=#3366CC>Heard Island and McDonald Islands</color>, but is otherwise the same as the UN definition, and it is also used
for statistical purposes.

In countries such as <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, <color=#3366CC>China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>, <color=#3366CC>Costa Rica</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ecuador</color>, <color=#3366CC>France</color>, <color=#3366CC>Greece</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Netherlands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Peru</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, <color=#3366CC>Switzerland</color> and <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>, Oceania is treated as a continent in the sense that it is "one of
the parts of the world", and Australia is only seen as an island nation. In other countries, including <color=#3366CC>Kazakhstan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Poland</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>, Australia and <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> are thought of as continents, while Asia, Europe and Oceania are regarded as "parts
of the world". In the Pacific Ocean Handbook (1945), author Eliot Grinnell Mears wrote that he categorized Australia,
New Zealand and Pacific islands under the label of Oceania for "scientific reasons; Australia's fauna is largely
continental in character, New Zealand's are clearly insular; and neither <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth realm</color> has close ties with Asia."
He further added that, "the term Australasia is not relished by New Zealanders and this name is too often confused with
Australia." Some 19th century definitions of Oceania grouped Australia, New Zealand and the islands of Melanesia
together under the label of Australasia, in other 19th century definitions of Oceania, the term was only used to refer to
Australia itself, with New Zealand being categorized with the islands of Polynesia in such definitions.
Archaeological terminology for this region has changed repeatedly. Before the 1970s, the single Pleistocene landmass
was called Australasia, derived from the <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> australis, meaning "southern", although this word is most often used for a
wider region that includes lands like New Zealand that are not on the same continental shelf. In the early 1970s, the
term Greater Australia was introduced for the Pleistocene continent. Then at a 1975 conference and consequent
publication, the name Sahul was extended from its previous use for just the Sahul Shelf to cover the continent.
In 1984, the name Meganesia was suggested, meaning "great island" or "great island-group", for both the Pleistocene
continent and the present-day lands, and this name has been widely accepted by biologists. Others have used
Meganesia with different meanings: travel writer Paul Theroux included New Zealand in his definition and others have
used it for Australia, New Zealand and <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color>. Another biologist, <color=#3366CC>Richard Dawkins</color>, coined the name Australinea in
2004. Australia–New Guinea has also been used.
History
The Australian continent and Sunda were points of early human migrations after leaving Africa. Research points to a
planned migration of hundreds of people using bamboo rafts, which eventually landed on Sahul.
Indigenous peoples
Indigenous Australians, that is <color=#3366CC>Aboriginal Australians</color> and <color=#3366CC>Torres Strait Islanders</color> people, are the original inhabitants of
the Australian continent and nearby islands. They migrated from Africa to Asia around 70,000 years ago and arrived in
Australia at least 50,000 years ago, based on archaeological evidence. More recent research points to earlier arrival,
possibly 65,000 years ago.
They are believed to be among the <color=#3366CC>earliest human migrations out of Africa</color>. There is evidence of genetic and linguistic
interchange between Australians in the far north and the Austronesian peoples of modern-day <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color> and the
islands, but this may be the result of recent trade and <color=#3366CC>intermarriage</color>. The earliest known human remains were found at
Lake Mungo, a dry lake in the southwest of New South Wales. Remains found at Mungo suggest one of the world's
oldest known <color=#3366CC>cremations</color>, thus indicating early evidence for religious ritual among humans. <color=#3366CC>Dreamtime</color> remains a
prominent feature of <color=#3366CC>Australian Aboriginal art</color>, the oldest continuing tradition of art in the world.
<color=#3366CC>Papuan</color> habitation is estimated to have begun between 42,000 and 48,000 years ago in New Guinea. Trade between
New Guinea and neighboring Indonesian islands was documented as early as the seventh century, and archipelagic
rule of New Guinea by the 13th. At the beginning of the seventh century, the <color=#3366CC>Sumatra</color>-based empire of <color=#3366CC>Srivijaya</color> (7th
century–13th century) engaged in trade relations with western New Guinea, initially taking items like <color=#3366CC>sandalwood</color> and
<color=#3366CC>birds-of-paradise</color> in tribute to China, but later making slaves out of the natives. The rule of the <color=#3366CC>Java</color>-based empire of
<color=#3366CC>Majapahit</color> (1293–1527) extended to the western fringes of New Guinea. Recent archaeological research suggests that
50,000 years ago people may have occupied sites in the highlands at New Guinean altitudes of up to 2000 m, rather
than being restricted to warmer coastal areas.
Pre-colonial history
Legends of Terra Australis Incognita—an "unknown land of the South"—date back to Roman times and before, and
were commonplace in medieval geography, although not based on any documented knowledge of the continent.
Ancient Greek philosopher <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> speculated of a large landmass in the southern hemisphere, saying, "Now since
there must be a region bearing the same relation to the southern pole as the place we live in bears to our pole...". His
ideas were later expanded by <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color> (2nd century AD), who believed that the lands of the <color=#3366CC>Northern Hemisphere</color>
should be balanced by land in the <color=#3366CC>south</color>. The theory of balancing land has been documented as early as the 5th
century on maps by Macrobius, who uses the term Australis on his maps.
Terra Australis, a hypothetical <color=#3366CC>continent</color> first posited in <color=#3366CC>antiquity</color>, appeared on maps between the 15th and 18th
centuries. Scientists, such as <color=#3366CC>Gerardus Mercator</color> (1569) and Alexander Dalrymple as late as 1767 argued for its
existence, with such arguments as that there should be a large landmass in the <color=#3366CC>south</color> as a counterweight to the known
landmasses in the Northern Hemisphere. The cartographic depictions of the southern continent in the 16th and early
17th centuries, as might be expected for a concept based on such abundant conjecture and minimal data, varied wildly
from map to map; in general, the continent shrank as potential locations were reinterpreted. At its largest, the continent
included <color=#3366CC>Tierra del Fuego</color>, separated from South America by a small strait; <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color>; and what would come to be
called Australia.
European exploration
In 1606, Dutch navigator <color=#3366CC>Willem Janszoon</color> made the first documented European sight and landing on the continent of
Australia in <color=#3366CC>Cape York Peninsula</color>. Dutch explorer <color=#3366CC>Abel Janszoon Tasman</color> circumnavigated and landed on parts of the
<color=#3366CC>Australian</color> continental coast and discovered Van Diemen's Land (now <color=#3366CC>Tasmania</color>), <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color> in 1642, and <color=#3366CC>Fiji</color>
islands. He was the first known European explorer to reach these islands.
In the quest for Terra Australis, Spanish explorations in the 17th century, such as the expedition led by the Portuguese

navigator <color=#3366CC>Pedro Fernandes de Queirós</color>, discovered the <color=#3366CC>Pitcairn</color> and <color=#3366CC>Vanuatu</color> archipelagos, and sailed the <color=#3366CC>Torres Strait</color>
between <color=#3366CC>Australia</color> and <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color>, named after navigator <color=#3366CC>Luís Vaz de Torres</color>, who was the first European to explore
the Strait. When <color=#3366CC>Europeans</color> first arrived, inhabitants of New Guinea and nearby islands, whose technologies included
bone, wood, and stone tools, had a productive agricultural system. In 1660, the Dutch recognised the Sultan of <color=#3366CC>Tidore</color>'s
sovereignty over <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color>. The first known Europeans to sight New Guinea were probably the <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> navigators sailing in the South Pacific in the early part of the 16th century.
On 23 April 1770, British explorer <color=#3366CC>James Cook</color> made his first recorded direct observation of indigenous Australians at
Brush Island near Bawley Point. On 29 April, Cook and crew made their first landfall on the mainland of the continent at
a place now known as the Kurnell Peninsula. It is here that James Cook made first contact with an Aboriginal tribe
known as the Gweagal, who he fired upon, injuring one. His expedition became the first recorded Europeans to have
encountered the eastern coastline of Australia. Captain <color=#3366CC>Arthur Phillip</color> led the <color=#3366CC>First Fleet</color> of 11 ships and about 850
convicts into <color=#3366CC>Sydney</color> on 26 January 1788. This was to be the location for the new colony. Phillip described Sydney
Cove as being "without exception the finest harbour in the world".
Modern history
In 1883, the <color=#3366CC>Colony of Queensland</color> tried to annex the southern half of eastern New Guinea, but the British government
did approve. The <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth of Australia</color> came into being when the Federal Constitution was proclaimed by the
Governor-General, Lord Hopetoun, on 1 January 1901. From that point a system of federalism in Australia came into
operation, entailing the establishment of an entirely new national government (the Commonwealth government) and an
ongoing division of powers between that government and the States. With the encouragement of Queensland, in 1884,
a British protectorate had been proclaimed over the southern coast of New Guinea and its adjacent islands. British New
Guinea was annexed outright in 1888. The possession was placed under the authority of the newly federated
Commonwealth of Australia in 1902 and with passage of the Papua Act 1905, British New Guinea became the
Australian Territory of Papua, with formal Australian administration beginning in 1906.
The Bombing of Darwin on 19 February 1942 was the largest single attack ever mounted by a foreign power on
Australia. In an effort to isolate Australia, the Japanese planned a seaborne invasion of <color=#3366CC>Port Moresby</color>, in the Australian
<color=#3366CC>Territory of New Guinea</color>. Between July and November 1942, Australian forces repulsed Japanese attempts on the city
by way of the <color=#3366CC>Kokoda Track</color>, in the highlands of <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color>. The Battle of Buna–Gona, between November 1942 and
January 1943, set the tone for the bitter final stages of the New Guinea campaign, which persisted into 1945. The
offensives in Papua and New Guinea of 1943–44 were the single largest series of connected operations ever mounted
by the Australian armed forces.
Following the 1998 commencement of reforms across Indonesia, Papua and other Indonesian provinces received
greater regional autonomy. In 2001, "Special Autonomy" status was granted to Papua province, although to date,
implementation has been partial and often criticised. The region was administered as a single province until 2003,
when it was split into the provinces of <color=#3366CC>Papua</color> and <color=#3366CC>West Papua</color>. Elections in 1972 resulted in the formation of a ministry
headed by Chief Minister <color=#3366CC>Michael Somare</color>, who pledged to lead the country to self-government and then to
independence. Papua New Guinea became self-governing on 1 December 1973 and achieved independence on 16
September 1975. The country joined the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> (UN) on 10 October 1975.
Migration brought large numbers of southern and central Europeans to Australia for the first time. A 1958 government
leaflet assured readers that unskilled non-British migrants were needed for "labour on rugged projects ...work which is
not generally acceptable to Australians or British workers". Australia fought on the side of Britain in the two <color=#3366CC>world wars</color>
and became a long-standing <color=#3366CC>ally of the United States</color> when threatened by <color=#3366CC>Imperial Japan</color> during <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>. Trade
with Asia increased and a post-war immigration program received more than 6.5 million migrants from every continent.
Supported by immigration of people from more than 200 countries since the end of World War II, the population
increased to more than 23 million by 2014.
Geography
The Australian continent, as a whole being part of the Australian Plate, is the lowest, flattest, and oldest landmass on
Earth and it has had a relatively stable geological history. <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color> is not part of the continent of Australia, but of
the separate, submerged continent of <color=#3366CC>Zealandia</color>. New Zealand and Australia are both part of the Oceanian sub-region
known as <color=#3366CC>Australasia</color>, with New Guinea being in <color=#3366CC>Melanesia</color>.
The continent includes a continental shelf overlain by shallow seas which divide it into several landmasses—the
<color=#3366CC>Arafura Sea</color> and <color=#3366CC>Torres Strait</color> between mainland Australia and New Guinea, and <color=#3366CC>Bass Strait</color> between mainland
Australia and Tasmania. When <color=#3366CC>sea levels</color> were lower during the <color=#3366CC>Pleistocene ice age</color>, including the <color=#3366CC>Last Glacial</color>
<color=#3366CC>Maximum</color> about 18,000 BC, they were connected by dry land.
During the past 18,000 to 10,000 years, rising sea levels overflowed the lowlands and separated the continent into
today's low-lying arid to <color=#3366CC>semi-arid</color> mainland and the two mountainous islands of New Guinea and Tasmania. The
<color=#3366CC>continental shelf</color> connecting the islands, half of which is less than 50 m deep, covers some 2.5 e6km2, including the
Sahul Shelf and <color=#3366CC>Bass Strait</color>.
Geological forces such as <color=#3366CC>tectonic uplift</color> of mountain ranges or clashes between tectonic plates occurred mainly in
Australia's early history, when it was still a part of <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color>. Australia is situated in the middle of the tectonic plate,
and therefore currently has no active volcanism.
The continent primarily sits on the Indo-Australian Plate. Because of its central location on its tectonic plate, Australia
does not have any active volcanic regions, the only continent with this distinction. The lands were joined with <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>
as part of the southern supercontinent <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color> until the plate began to drift north about 96 million years ago.
For most of the time since then, Australia–New Guinea remained a continuous landmass. When the <color=#3366CC>last glacial period</color>
ended in about 10,000 BC, rising sea levels formed <color=#3366CC>Bass Strait</color>, separating Tasmania from the mainland. Then
between about 8,000 and 6,500 BC, the lowlands in the north were flooded by the sea, separating the <color=#3366CC>Aru Islands</color>,
mainland Australia, <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color>, and Tasmania.
A northern arc consisting of the <color=#3366CC>New Guinea Highlands</color>, the Raja Ampat Islands, and <color=#3366CC>Halmahera</color> was uplifted by the
northward migration of Australia and subduction of the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Plate</color>. The Outer Banda Arc was accreted along the
northwestern edge the continent; it includes the islands of <color=#3366CC>Timor</color>, Tanimbar, and <color=#3366CC>Seram</color>. Papua New Guinea has
several volcanoes, as it is situated along the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ring of Fire</color>. Volcanic eruptions are not rare, and the area is prone
to <color=#3366CC>earthquakes</color> and <color=#3366CC>tsunamis</color> because of this. Mount Wilhelm in Papua New Guinea is the second highest mountain in
the continent, and at 4884 m <color=#3366CC>above sea level</color>, <color=#3366CC>Puncak Jaya</color> is the highest mountain.
Ecology
Flora
For about 40 million years Australia–New Guinea was almost completely isolated. During this time, the continent
experienced numerous changes in climate, but the overall trend was towards greater aridity. When <color=#3366CC>South America</color>
eventually separated from Antarctica, the development of the cold Antarctic Circumpolar Current changed weather
patterns across the world. For Australia–New Guinea, it brought a marked intensification of the drying trend. The great
inland seas and lakes dried out. Much of the long-established broad-leaf deciduous forest began to give way to the
distinctive hard-leaved sclerophyllous plants that characterise the modern Australian landscape.
Typical Southern Hemisphere flora include the <color=#3366CC>conifers</color> <color=#3366CC>Podocarpus</color> (eastern Australia and New Guinea), the rainforest
emergents Araucaria (eastern Australia and New Guinea), <color=#3366CC>Nothofagus</color> (New Guinea and <color=#3366CC>Tasmania</color>) and Agathis
(northern <color=#3366CC>Queensland</color> and New Guinea), as well as tree ferns and several species of Eucalyptus. Prominent features of
the Australian flora are adaptations to aridity and fire which include scleromorphy and serotiny. These adaptations are
common in species from the large and well-known families <color=#3366CC>Proteaceae</color> (<color=#3366CC>Banksias</color> and Grevilleas), <color=#3366CC>Myrtaceae</color>
(<color=#3366CC>Eucalyptus</color> or gum trees, Melaleucas and Callistemons), <color=#3366CC>Fabaceae</color> (<color=#3366CC>Acacia</color>s or wattles), and Casuarinaceae
(Casuarinas or she-oaks), which are typically found in the Australian mainland. The flora of New Guinea is a mixture of
many <color=#3366CC>tropical rainforest</color> species with origins in Asia, such as Castanopsis acuminatissima, <color=#3366CC>Lithocarpus</color> spp.,
elaeocarps, and <color=#3366CC>laurels</color>, together with typically Australasian flora. In the New Guinean highlands, conifers such as
Dacrycarpus, Dacrydium, Papuacedrus and Libocedrus are present.
For many species, the primary refuge was the relatively cool and well-watered <color=#3366CC>Great Dividing Range</color>. Even today,
pockets of remnant vegetation remain in the cool uplands, some species not much changed from the Gondwanan
forms of 60 or 90 million years ago. Eventually, the Australia–New Guinea tectonic plate collided with the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian</color>
<color=#3366CC>plate</color> to the north. The collision caused the northern part of the continent to buckle upwards, forming the high and
rugged mountains of New Guinea and, by reverse (downwards) buckling, the <color=#3366CC>Torres Strait</color> that now separates the two
main landmasses. The collision also pushed up the islands of Wallacea, which served as island 'stepping-stones' that
allowed plants from <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>'s rainforests to colonise New Guinea, and some plants from Australia–New Guinea
to move into Southeast Asia. The ocean straits between the islands were narrow enough to allow plant dispersal, but
served as an effective barrier to exchange of land mammals between Australia–New Guinea and Asia. Among the
fungi, the remarkable association between Cyttaria gunnii (one of the "golf-ball" fungi) and its associated trees in the
genus <color=#3366CC>Nothofagus</color> is evidence of that drift: the only other places where this association is known are New Zealand and
southern <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> and <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>.
Fauna
Due to the spread of animals, fungi and plants across the single Pleistocene landmass the separate lands have a
related <color=#3366CC>biota</color>. There are over 300 bird species in <color=#3366CC>West Papua</color>, of which at least 20 are unique to the ecoregion, and
some live only in very restricted areas. These include the grey-banded munia, Vogelkop bowerbird, and the king
bird-of-paradise.
Australia has a huge variety of animals; some 83% of mammals, 89% of reptiles, 24% of fish and insects and 93% of
<color=#3366CC>amphibians</color> that inhabit the continent are <color=#3366CC>endemic</color> to Australia. This high level of endemism can be attributed to the
continent's long geographic isolation, <color=#3366CC>tectonic</color> stability, and the effects of an unusual pattern of climate change on the
soil and flora over geological time. Australia and its territories are home to around 800 species of bird; 45% of these are
endemic to Australia. Predominant bird species in Australia include the <color=#3366CC>Australian magpie</color>, Australian raven, the pied

currawong, crested pigeons and the laughing kookaburra. The <color=#3366CC>koala</color>, <color=#3366CC>emu</color>, <color=#3366CC>platypus</color> and <color=#3366CC>kangaroo</color> are national animals
of Australia, and the <color=#3366CC>Tasmanian devil</color> is also one of the well-known animals in the country. The goanna is a <color=#3366CC>predatory</color>
lizard native to the Australian mainland.
As the continent drifted north from Antarctica, a unique fauna, flora and <color=#3366CC>mycobiota</color> developed. <color=#3366CC>Marsupials</color> and
<color=#3366CC>monotremes</color> also existed on other continents, but only in Australia–New Guinea did they out-compete the <color=#3366CC>placental</color>
<color=#3366CC>mammals</color> and come to dominate. New Guinea has 284 species and six orders of mammals: monotremes, three orders
of marsupials, <color=#3366CC>rodents</color> and <color=#3366CC>bats</color>; 195 of the mammal species (69%) are endemic. New Guinea has a rich diversity of
<color=#3366CC>coral</color> life and 1,200 species of <color=#3366CC>fish</color> have been found. Also about 600 species of reef-building coral—the latter equal to
75 percent of the world's known total. New Guinea has 578 species of breeding birds, of which 324 species are
endemic. <color=#3366CC>Bird</color> life also flourished—in particular, the <color=#3366CC>songbirds</color> (order <color=#3366CC>Passeriformes</color>, suborder Passeri) are thought to
have evolved 50 million years ago in the part of <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color> that later became <color=#3366CC>Australia</color>, New Zealand, <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>, before radiating into a great number of different forms and then spreading around the globe.
Animal groups such as macropods, <color=#3366CC>monotremes</color>, and <color=#3366CC>cassowaries</color> are endemic to Australia. There were three main
reasons for the enormous diversity that developed in animal, fungal and plant life.
• While much of the rest of the world underwent significant cooling and thus loss of species diversity, Australia–New
Guinea was drifting north at such a pace that the overall global cooling effect was roughly equalled by its gradual
movement toward the <color=#3366CC>equator</color>. <color=#3366CC>Temperatures</color> in Australia–New Guinea, in other words, remained reasonably
constant for a very long time, and a vast number of different animal, fungal and plant species were able to evolve to
fit particular <color=#3366CC>ecological niches</color>. Because the continent was more isolated than any other, very few outside species
arrived to colonise, and unique native forms developed unimpeded.
• Finally, despite the fact that the continent was already very old and thus relatively infertile, there are dispersed
areas of high fertility. Where other continents had <color=#3366CC>volcanic</color> activity and/or massive <color=#3366CC>glaciation</color> events to turn over
fresh, unleached <color=#3366CC>rocks</color> rich in <color=#3366CC>minerals</color>, the rocks and <color=#3366CC>soils</color> of Australia–New Guinea were left largely untouched
except by gradual <color=#3366CC>erosion</color> and deep <color=#3366CC>weathering</color>. In general, fertile soils produce a profusion of life, and a relatively
large number of species/level of biodiversity. This is because where <color=#3366CC>nutrients</color> are plentiful, competition is largely a
matter of outcompeting rival species, leaving great scope for innovative <color=#3366CC>co-evolution</color> as is witnessed in tropical,
fertile ecosystems. In contrast, infertile soils tend to induce competition on an abiotic basis meaning individuals all
face constant environmental pressures, leaving less scope for divergent evolution, a process instrumental in
creating new species.
Although New Guinea is the most northerly part of the continent, and could be expected to be the most <color=#3366CC>tropical</color> in
climate, the altitude of the New Guinea highlands is such that a great many animals and plants that were once common
across Australia–New Guinea now survive only in the tropical highlands where they are severely threatened by
<color=#3366CC>population growth</color>.
Climate
In New Guinea, the climate is mostly <color=#3366CC>monsoonal</color> (December to March), southeast monsoon (May to October), and
<color=#3366CC>tropical rainforest</color> with slight seasonal temperature variation. In lower altitudes, the temperature is around 27 C year
round. But the higher altitudes, such as Mendi, are constantly around 21 C with cool lows nearing 11 C, with abundant
rainfall and high humidity. The <color=#3366CC>New Guinea Highlands</color> are one of the few regions close to the <color=#3366CC>equator</color> that experience
<color=#3366CC>snowfall</color>, which occurs in the most elevated parts of the mainland. Some areas in the island experience an
extraordinary amount of precipitation, averaging roughly 4500 mm of rainfall annually.
The Australian landmass's climate is mostly <color=#3366CC>desert</color> or <color=#3366CC>semi-arid</color>, with the southern coastal corners having a <color=#3366CC>temperate</color>
climate, such as oceanic and <color=#3366CC>humid subtropical</color> climate in the east coast and <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean climate</color> in the west. The
northern parts of the country have a <color=#3366CC>tropical climate</color>. <color=#3366CC>Snow</color> falls frequently on the <color=#3366CC>highlands</color> near the east coast, in the

states of <color=#3366CC>Victoria</color>, <color=#3366CC>New South Wales</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tasmania</color> and in the <color=#3366CC>Australian Capital Territory</color>. Temperatures in Australia have
ranged from above 50 C to well below 0 C. Nonetheless, minimum temperatures are moderated. The <color=#3366CC>El Niño-Southern</color>
<color=#3366CC>Oscillation</color> is associated with seasonal abnormality in many areas in the world. Australia is one of the continents most
affected and experiences extensive droughts alongside considerable wet periods.
Politics

Australia is a <color=#3366CC>federal</color> <color=#3366CC>parliamentary</color> <color=#3366CC>constitutional monarchy</color> with <color=#3366CC>Charles III</color> at its apex as the King of Australia, a role
that is distinct from his position as monarch of the other Commonwealth realms. The King is represented in Australia by
the Governor-General at the federal level and by the Governors at the state level, who by convention act on the advice
of the government's ministers. There are two major political groups that usually form government, federally and in the
states: the Australian Labor Party and the Coalition which is a formal grouping of the Liberal Party and its minor
partner, the National Party. Within Australian political culture, the Coalition is considered <color=#3366CC>centre-right</color> and the Labor
Party is considered <color=#3366CC>centre-left</color>.
Papua New Guinea is a Commonwealth realm. As such, King <color=#3366CC>Charles III</color> is its sovereign and head of state. The
constitutional convention, which prepared the draft constitution, and Australia, the outgoing metropolitan power, had
thought that Papua New Guinea would not remain a monarchy. The founders, however, considered that imperial
honours had a cachet. The monarch is represented by the Governor-General of Papua New Guinea, currently Bob
Dadae. Papua New Guinea (along with <color=#3366CC>Solomon Islands</color>) is unusual among Commonwealth realms in that
governors-general are elected by the legislature, rather than chosen by the executive branch.
Economy
Australia is the only <color=#3366CC>First World</color> country on the Australia-New Guinea continent, although the <color=#3366CC>economy of Australia</color> is by
far the largest and most dominant economy in the region and one of the largest in the world. Australia's per-capita GDP

is higher than that of the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>, <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, and <color=#3366CC>France</color> in terms of <color=#3366CC>purchasing power parity</color>. The
Australian Securities Exchange in <color=#3366CC>Sydney</color> is the largest stock exchange in Australia and in the South Pacific. In 2012,
Australia was the 12th largest national economy by nominal GDP and the 19th-largest measured by <color=#3366CC>PPP-adjusted</color>
GDP.
Tourism in Australia is an important component of the Australian economy. In the financial year 2014/15, <color=#3366CC>tourism</color>
represented 3.0% of <color=#3366CC>Australia</color>'s <color=#3366CC>GDP</color> contributing A$47.5 billion to the national economy. In 2015, there were 7.4
million visitor arrivals. Mercer Quality of Living Survey ranks Sydney tenth in the world in terms of <color=#3366CC>quality of living</color>,
making it one of the most livable cities. It is classified as an Alpha+ <color=#3366CC>World City</color> by GaWC. <color=#3366CC>Melbourne</color> also ranked highly
in the world's most liveable city list, and is a leading financial centre in the Asia-Pacific region.
Papua New Guinea is rich in natural resources, which account for two-thirds of their export earnings. Though PNG is
filled with resources, the lack of country's development led foreign countries to take over few sites and continued
foreign demand for PNG's resources and as a result, the United States constructed an oil company and began to
export in 2004 and this was the largest project in PNG's history. Papua New Guinea is classified as a <color=#3366CC>developing</color>
<color=#3366CC>economy</color> by the <color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color>. Strong growth in Papua New Guinea's mining and resource sector led to
the country becoming the sixth fastest-growing economy in the world in 2011.
Demographics
Immigration
Since 1945, more than 7 million people have settled in Australia. From the late 1970s, there was a significant increase
in immigration from Asian and other non-European countries, making Australia a multicultural country. Sydney is the
most <color=#3366CC>multicultural</color> city in Oceania, having more than 250 different languages spoken, with about 40 percent of residents
speaking a language other than English at home. Furthermore, 36 percent of the population reported having been born

overseas, with top countries being <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> and <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>, among others. <color=#3366CC>Melbourne</color> is also fairly
multicultural, having the largest Greek-speaking population outside of <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, and the second largest Asian population
in Australia after Sydney.
Religion
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> is the predominant religion in the continent, although large proportions of Australians belong to <color=#3366CC>no religion</color>.
Other religions in the region include <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>, which are prominent minority religions in Australia.
Traditional religions are often <color=#3366CC>animist</color>, found in New Guinea. <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> is widespread in the <color=#3366CC>Indonesian New Guinea</color>. Many
Papuans combine their Christian faith with traditional indigenous beliefs and practices.
Languages
"<color=#3366CC>Aboriginal Australian languages</color>", including the large Pama–Nyungan family, "Papuan languages" of <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color> and
neighbouring islands, including the large <color=#3366CC>Trans–New Guinea</color> family, and "Tasmanian languages" are generic terms for
the native languages of the continent other than those of <color=#3366CC>Austronesian</color> family. Predominant languages include <color=#3366CC>English</color>
in Australia, <color=#3366CC>Tok Pisin</color> in Papua New Guinea, and <color=#3366CC>Indonesian</color> (Malay) in Indonesian New Guinea. Immigration to

Australia have brought overseas languages such as <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Greek</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Filipino</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mandarin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Vietnamese</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Spanish</color>, among others. Contact between Austronesian and Papuan resulted in several instances in <color=#3366CC>mixed languages</color>
such as Maisin. <color=#3366CC>Tok Pisin</color> is an English <color=#3366CC>creole language</color> spoken in Papua New Guinea. Papua New Guinea has more
languages than any other country, with over 820 indigenous languages, representing 12% of the world's total, but most
have fewer than 1,000 speakers.
Culture
Since 1788, the primary influence behind Australian culture has been Anglo-Celtic <color=#3366CC>Western culture</color>, with some
Indigenous influences. The divergence and evolution that has occurred in the ensuing centuries has resulted in a
distinctive Australian culture. Since the mid-20th century, <color=#3366CC>American popular culture</color> has strongly influenced Australia,
particularly through television and cinema. Other cultural influences come from neighbouring Asian countries, and
through large-scale immigration from non-English-speaking nations. The Australian Museum in Sydney and the
National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne are the oldest and largest <color=#3366CC>museums</color> in the continent, as well as in <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color>.
Sydney's New Year's Eve celebrations are the largest in the continent.
It is estimated that more than 7,000 different cultural groups exist in Papua New Guinea, and most groups have their
own language. Because of this diversity, in which they take pride, many different styles of cultural expression have
emerged; each group has created its own expressive forms in <color=#3366CC>art</color>, <color=#3366CC>performance art</color>, <color=#3366CC>weaponry</color>, <color=#3366CC>costumes</color> and
<color=#3366CC>architecture</color>. Papua New Guinea is one of the few cultures in Oceania to practice the tradition of <color=#3366CC>bride price</color>. In
particular, Papua New Guinea is world-famous for carved wooden <color=#3366CC>sculpture</color>: masks, canoes, story-boards.
Australia has a tradition of Aboriginal art which is thousands of years old, the best known forms being rock art and bark
painting. Evidence of <color=#3366CC>Aboriginal art</color> in Australia can be traced back at least 30,000 years. Examples of ancient
Aboriginal rock artworks can be found throughout the continent – notably in national parks such as those of the
<color=#3366CC>UNESCO</color> listed sites at <color=#3366CC>Uluru</color> and <color=#3366CC>Kakadu National Park</color> in the Northern Territory, but also within protected parks in
urban areas such as at Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park in Sydney. Aboriginal culture includes a number of practices
and ceremonies centered on a belief in the <color=#3366CC>Dreamtime</color>. Reverence for the land and oral traditions are emphasised.
Sport

Popular sports in Papua New Guinea include various codes of <color=#3366CC>football</color> (<color=#3366CC>rugby league</color>, <color=#3366CC>rugby union</color>, <color=#3366CC>soccer</color>, and

<color=#3366CC>Australian rules football</color>), <color=#3366CC>cricket</color>, <color=#3366CC>volleyball</color>, <color=#3366CC>softball</color>, <color=#3366CC>netball</color>, and <color=#3366CC>basketball</color>. Other <color=#3366CC>Olympic sports</color> are also gaining
popularity, such as <color=#3366CC>boxing</color> and <color=#3366CC>weightlifting</color>. <color=#3366CC>Rugby league</color> is the most popular sport in Papua New Guinea (especially
in the highlands), which also unofficially holds the title as the national sport. The most popular sport in Australia is
<color=#3366CC>cricket</color>, the most popular sport among Australian women is <color=#3366CC>netball</color>, while <color=#3366CC>Australian rules football</color> is the most popular
sport in terms of spectatorship and television ratings. Australia has hosted two Summer Olympic Games: Melbourne
1956 and Sydney 2000. Australia has also hosted five editions of the <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth Games</color> (Sydney 1938, Perth
1962, Brisbane 1982, Melbourne 2006, and Gold Coast 2018). In 2006 Australia joined the Asian Football
Confederation and qualified for the 2010 and 2014 World Cups as an Asian entrant.
Cobalt
Cobalt is a <color=#3366CC>chemical element</color>; it has symbol Co and <color=#3366CC>atomic number</color> 27. As with <color=#3366CC>nickel</color>, cobalt is found in the Earth's
crust only in a chemically combined form, save for small deposits found in alloys of natural <color=#3366CC>meteoric iron</color>. The free
element, produced by reductive <color=#3366CC>smelting</color>, is a hard, lustrous, somewhat brittle, gray <color=#3366CC>metal</color>.
Cobalt-based blue pigments (cobalt blue) have been used since antiquity for jewelry and paints, and to impart a
distinctive blue tint to glass. The color was long thought to be due to the metal <color=#3366CC>bismuth</color>. Miners had long used the name
kobold ore (<color=#3366CC>German</color> for <color=#3366CC>goblin</color> ore) for some of the blue pigment-producing <color=#3366CC>minerals</color>. They were so named because
they were poor in known metals and gave off poisonous <color=#3366CC>arsenic</color>-containing fumes when smelted. In 1735, such ores
were found to be reducible to a new metal (the first discovered since ancient times), which was ultimately named for the
kobold.
Today, cobalt is usually produced as a by-product of <color=#3366CC>copper</color> and nickel mining, but sometimes also from one of a
number of metallic-lustered ores such as <color=#3366CC>cobaltite</color> (CoAsS). The Copperbelt in the <color=#3366CC>Democratic Republic of the Congo</color>
(DRC) and <color=#3366CC>Zambia</color> yields most of the global cobalt production. World production in 2016 was 116,000 t according to
Natural Resources Canada, and the DRC alone accounted for more than 50%. In 2024, production exceeded 300,000
tons, of which DRC accounted for more than 80%.
Cobalt is primarily used in <color=#3366CC>lithium-ion batteries</color>, and in the manufacture of <color=#3366CC>magnetic</color>, wear-resistant and high-strength
<color=#3366CC>alloys</color>. The compounds cobalt silicate and cobalt(II) aluminate (CoAl2O4, cobalt blue) give a distinctive deep blue color

to <color=#3366CC>glass</color>, <color=#3366CC>ceramics</color>, <color=#3366CC>inks</color>, <color=#3366CC>paints</color> and <color=#3366CC>varnishes</color>. Cobalt occurs naturally as only one stable <color=#3366CC>isotope</color>, cobalt-59. <color=#3366CC>Cobalt-60</color>
is a commercially important radioisotope, used as a radioactive tracer and for the production of high-energy <color=#3366CC>gamma</color>
<color=#3366CC>rays</color>. Cobalt is also used in the petroleum industry as a catalyst when refining crude oil. This is to purge it of sulfur,
which is very polluting when burned and causes <color=#3366CC>acid rain</color>.
Cobalt is the active center of a group of coenzymes called <color=#3366CC>cobalamins</color>, also known as <color=#3366CC>Vitamin B12</color>, which is an

essential <color=#3366CC>vitamin</color> for all animals. Cobalt in inorganic form is also a micronutrient for <color=#3366CC>bacteria</color>, <color=#3366CC>algae</color>, and <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>.
The name cobalt derives from a type of ore considered a nuisance by 16th-century German silver miners, which in turn
may have been named from a spirit or goblin held superstitiously responsible for it; this spirit is considered equitable to
the kobold (a household spirit) by some, or categorized as a <color=#3366CC>gnome</color> (mine spirit) by others.
Characteristics
Cobalt is a <color=#3366CC>ferromagnetic</color> metal with a <color=#3366CC>specific gravity</color> of 8.9. The <color=#3366CC>Curie temperature</color> is 1115 C and the magnetic

moment is 1.6–1.7 <color=#3366CC>Bohr magnetons</color> per <color=#3366CC>atom</color>. Cobalt has a <color=#3366CC>relative permeability</color> two-thirds that of <color=#3366CC>iron</color>. <color=#3366CC>Metallic</color> cobalt
occurs as two <color=#3366CC>crystallographic structures</color>: hcp and <color=#3366CC>fcc</color>. The ideal transition temperature between the hcp and fcc
structures is 450 C, but in practice the energy difference between them is so small that random intergrowth of the two is
common.

Cobalt is a weakly reducing metal that is protected from <color=#3366CC>oxidation</color> by a <color=#3366CC>passivating</color> <color=#3366CC>oxide</color> film. It is attacked by <color=#3366CC>halogens</color>
and <color=#3366CC>sulfur</color>. Heating in <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color> produces Co3O4 which loses oxygen at 900 C to give the monoxide CoO. The metal

reacts with <color=#3366CC>fluorine</color> (F2) at 520 K to give CoF3; with <color=#3366CC>chlorine</color> (Cl2), <color=#3366CC>bromine</color> (Br2) and <color=#3366CC>iodine</color> (I2), producing equivalent
binary <color=#3366CC>halides</color>. It does not react with <color=#3366CC>hydrogen gas</color> (H2) or <color=#3366CC>nitrogen gas</color> (N2) even when heated, but it does react with

<color=#3366CC>boron</color>, <color=#3366CC>carbon</color>, <color=#3366CC>phosphorus</color>, <color=#3366CC>arsenic</color> and sulfur. At ordinary temperatures, it reacts slowly with <color=#3366CC>mineral acids</color>, and very
slowly with moist, but not dry, air.
Compounds
Common <color=#3366CC>oxidation states</color> of cobalt include +2 and +3, although compounds with oxidation states ranging from 3 to +5
are also known. A common oxidation state for simple compounds is +2 (cobalt(II)). These salts form the pink-colored
metal aquo complex [Co(H2O)6]2+ in water. Addition of <color=#3366CC>chloride</color> gives the intensely blue [CoCl4]2-. In a borax bead
<color=#3366CC>flame test</color>, cobalt shows deep blue in both oxidizing and reducing flames.
Oxygen and chalcogen compounds
Several binary <color=#3366CC>oxides</color> of cobalt are known. Green cobalt(II) oxide (CoO) has <color=#3366CC>rocksalt</color> structure. It is readily oxidized with
water and oxygen to brown cobalt(III) hydroxide (Co(OH)3). At temperatures of 600–700 °C, CoO oxidizes to the blue
cobalt(II,III) oxide (Co3O4), which has a <color=#3366CC>spinel structure</color>. Black cobalt(III) oxide (Co2O3) is also known. Cobalt oxides
are <color=#3366CC>antiferromagnetic</color> at low <color=#3366CC>temperature</color>: CoO (<color=#3366CC>Néel temperature</color> 291 K) and Co3O4 (Néel temperature: 40 K), which
is analogous to <color=#3366CC>magnetite</color> (Fe3O4), with a mixture of +2 and +3 oxidation states. Potassium percobaltate (K3CoO4)
contains a rare example of a cobalt(V) complex.
The principal <color=#3366CC>chalcogenides</color> of cobalt are the black cobalt(II) sulfides, CoS2 (<color=#3366CC>pyrite</color> structure), Co2S3 (<color=#3366CC>spinel structure</color>),
and CoS (nickel arsenide structure).
Halides
The salt caesium hexafluorocobaltate(IV) (Cs2CoF6) is a rare example of cobalt(IV). The reduction potential for the
reaction Co(3+) + e Co(2+) is +1.92 V, beyond that for <color=#3366CC>chlorine</color> to chloride, +1.36 V. Consequently, cobalt(III) chloride
would spontaneously reduce to cobalt(II) chloride and chlorine. Because the reduction potential for fluorine to fluoride is
so high, +2.87 V, cobalt(III) fluoride is one of the few simple stable cobalt(III) compounds. Cobalt(III) fluoride, which is
used in some fluorination reactions, reacts vigorously with water.
Four dihalides of cobalt(II) are known: cobalt(II) fluoride (CoF2, pink), cobalt(II) chloride (CoCl2, blue), cobalt(II)
bromide (CoBr2, green), cobalt(II) iodide (CoI2, blue-black). These halides also exist in hydrated forms. Whereas the
anhydrous dichloride is blue, the hydrate is red. The pink-colored cation hexaaquocobalt(II) [Co(H2O)6](2+) is found in
several routine cobalt salts such as the nitrate and sulfate.
Coordination complexes
A large inventory of complexes exists for cobalt(III) bound to ammonia and amines (called ammine complexes).
Examples include [Co(NH3)6](3+), [Co(NH3)5Cl](2+) (chloropentamminecobalt(III)), and cis- and
trans-[Co(NH3)4Cl2]+. The corresponding <color=#3366CC>ethylenediamine</color> complexes are also well known. Analogues are known

where the halides are replaced by <color=#3366CC>nitrite</color>, <color=#3366CC>hydroxide</color>, <color=#3366CC>carbonate</color>, etc. <color=#3366CC>Alfred Werner</color> worked extensively on these
complexes in his Nobel-prize winning work. The robustness of these complexes is demonstrated by the optical
resolution of tris(ethylenediamine)cobalt(III) ([Co(en)3]3+).
The unusually high oxidation state +IV of cobalt can be stabilized by ligands based on [B11H11](4-) in dark blue
colored crystals. <color=#3366CC>Softer</color> ligands like triphenylphosphine form complexes with Co(II) and Co(I), examples being bis- and
tris(triphenylphosphine)cobalt(I) chloride, CoCl2(PPh3)2 and CoCl(PPh3)3. These Co(I) and Co(II) complexes
represent a link to the organometallic complexes described below.
Organometallic compounds
Cobaltocene is a structural analog to <color=#3366CC>ferrocene</color>, with cobalt in place of iron. Cobaltocene is much more sensitive to
oxidation than ferrocene. Cobalt carbonyl (Co2(CO)8) is a <color=#3366CC>catalyst</color> in carbonylation and hydrosilylation reactions.
Vitamin B12 (see below) is an organometallic compound found in nature and is the only <color=#3366CC>vitamin</color> that contains a metal
atom. An example of an alkylcobalt complex in the otherwise uncommon +4 oxidation state of cobalt is the homoleptic
complex tetrakis(1-norbornyl)cobalt(IV) (Co(1-norb)4), a transition metal-alkyl complex that is notable for its resistance
to -hydrogen elimination, in accord with Bredt's rule. The cobalt(III) and cobalt(V) complexes [Li(THF)4]+[Co(1-norb)4]-
and [Co(1-norb)4]+[BF4]- are also known.
Isotopes
59Co is the only stable cobalt <color=#3366CC>isotope</color> and the only isotope that exists naturally on Earth. Twenty-two <color=#3366CC>radioisotopes</color>
have been characterized: the most stable, <color=#3366CC>60Co</color>, has a <color=#3366CC>half-life</color> of 5.2714 years; 57Co has a half-life of 271.81 days;
56Co has a half-life of 77.24 days; and 58Co has a half-life of 70.84 days. All the other <color=#3366CC>radioactive</color> isotopes of cobalt
have half-lives shorter than 18 hours, and in most cases shorter than 1 second. This element also has 4 <color=#3366CC>meta states</color>,
all of which have half-lives shorter than 15 minutes.
The isotopes of cobalt range from 50Co to 78Co. The primary <color=#3366CC>decay mode</color> for isotopes with atomic masses less than
that of the only stable isotope, 59Co, is electron capture and the primary mode of decay in isotopes with atomic mass
greater than that is <color=#3366CC>beta decay</color>. The primary <color=#3366CC>decay products</color> below 59Co are element 26 (iron) isotopes; above that the
decay products are element 28 (nickel) isotopes.
The 59Co nucleus is detectable using <color=#3366CC>nuclear magnetic resonance</color> and has a magnetic quadrupole moment. Among all
NMR active nuclei, 59Co has the largest chemical shift range and the chemical shift can be correlated with the
spectrochemical series. Resonances are observed over a range of 20000 ppm, the width of the signals being up to 20
kHz. A widely used standard is potassium hexacyanocobaltate (0.1M K3Co(CN)6 in D2O), which, due to its high
symmetry, has a rather small line width. Systems of low symmetry can yield broadened signals to an extent that
renders the signals unobservable in fluid phase NMR, but still observable in solid state NMR.
Etymology
Many different stories about the origin of the word "cobalt" have been proposed. In one version the element cobalt was
named after "kobelt", the name which 16th century German silver miners had given to a nuisance type of ore which
occurred that was corrosive and issued poisonous gas. Although such ores had been used for blue pigmentation since
antiquity, the Germans at that time did not have the technology to <color=#3366CC>smelt</color> the ore into metal (cf. below).
The authority on such kobelt ore (Latinized as cobaltum or cadmia) at the time was <color=#3366CC>Georgius Agricola</color>. He was also the
oft-quoted authority on the mine spirits called "kobel" (Latinized as cobalus or pl. cobali) in a separate work.
Agricola did not make a connection between the similarly named ore and spirit. However, a causal connection (ore
blamed on "kobel") was made by a contemporary, and a word origin connection (word "formed" from cobalus) made by
a late 18th century writer. Later, Grimms' dictionary (1868) noted the kobalt/kobelt ore was blamed on the mountain
spirit (Bergmännchen) which was also held responsible for "stealing the silver and putting out an ore that caused poor
mining atmosphere (Wetter) and other health hazards".
Grimms' dictionary entries equated the word "kobel" with "kobold", and listed it as a mere variant diminutive, but the
latter is defined in it as a household spirit. Some more recent commentators prefer to characterize the ore's namesake
kobelt (recté kobel) as a <color=#3366CC>gnome</color>.
The early 20th century Oxford English Dictionary (1st edition, 1908) upheld Grimm's etymology. However, by around
the same time in Germany, the alternate etymology not endorsed by Grimm (kob/kof "house, chamber" + walt "power,
ruler") was being proposed as more convincing.
Somewhat later, Paul Kretschmer (1928) explained that while this "house ruler" etymology was the proper one that
backed the original meaning of kobold as household spirit, a corruption later occurred introducing the idea of "mine
demon" to it. The present edition of the Etymologisches Wörterbuch (25th ed., 2012) under "kobold" lists the latter, not
Grimm's etymology, but still maintains, under its entry for "kobalt", that the cobalt ore may have gotten its name from "a
type of mine spirit/demon" (daemon metallicus) while stating that this is "apparently" the kobold.
Joseph William Mellor (1935) also stated that cobalt may derive from kobalos, though other theories had been
suggested.
Alternate theories
Several alternative etymologies that have been suggested, which may not involve a spirit (kobel or kobold) at all. Karl
Müller-Fraureuth conjectured that kobelt derived from Kübel, a bucket used in mining, frequently mentioned by
Agricola, namely the kobel/köbel (Latinized as modulus).
Another theory given by the Etymologisches Wörterbuch derives the term from kōbathium or rather cobathia ("arsenic
sulfide") which occurs as noxious fumes.
An etymology from Slavonic kowalti was suggested by Emanuel Merck (1902).
<color=#3366CC>W. W. Skeat</color> and J. Berendes construed as "parasite", i.e. as an ore parasitic to <color=#3366CC>nickel</color>, but this explanation is faulted for
its anachronism since nickel was not discovered until 1751.
History
Cobalt compounds have been used for centuries to impart a rich blue color to <color=#3366CC>glass</color>, <color=#3366CC>glazes</color>, and <color=#3366CC>ceramics</color>. Cobalt has
been detected in Egyptian sculpture, Persian jewelry from the third millennium BC, in the ruins of <color=#3366CC>Pompeii</color>, destroyed in
79 AD, and in China, dating from the <color=#3366CC>Tang dynasty</color> (618–907 AD) and the <color=#3366CC>Ming dynasty</color> (1368–1644 AD).
Cobalt has been used to color glass since the <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color>. The excavation of the Uluburun shipwreck yielded an ingot
of blue glass, cast during the 14th century BC. Blue glass from Egypt was either colored with copper, iron, or cobalt.
The oldest cobalt-colored glass is from the eighteenth dynasty of Egypt (1550–1292 BC). The Egyptians sourced this
cobalt from cobaltiferous alums found in Egypt's Western Oases.
One possible origin of the word cobalt is the 16th century German "kobald", a type of ore. The first attempts to smelt
those ores for copper or silver failed, yielding simply powder (cobalt(II) oxide) instead. Because the primary ores of
cobalt always contain arsenic, smelting the ore oxidized the arsenic into the highly toxic and volatile arsenic oxide,
adding to the notoriety of the ore. <color=#3366CC>Paracelsus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Georgius Agricola</color>, and Basil Valentine all referred to such silicates as
"cobalt".
Swedish chemist Georg Brandt (1694–1768) is credited with discovering cobalt c. 1735, showing it to be a previously
unknown element, distinct from bismuth and other traditional metals. Brandt called it a new "semi-metal", naming it for
the mineral from which he had extracted it. He showed that compounds of cobalt metal were the source of the blue
color in glass, which previously had been attributed to the bismuth found with cobalt. Cobalt became the first metal to
be discovered since the pre-historical period. All previously known metals (iron, copper, silver, gold, zinc, mercury, tin,
lead and bismuth) had no recorded discoverers.
During the 19th century, a significant part of the world's production of cobalt blue (a pigment made with cobalt
compounds and alumina) and smalt (cobalt glass powdered for use for pigment purposes in ceramics and painting)
was carried out at the Norwegian Blaafarveværket. The first mines for the production of smalt in the 16th century were
located in Norway, Sweden, <color=#3366CC>Saxony</color> and Hungary. With the discovery of cobalt ore in <color=#3366CC>New Caledonia</color> in 1864, the
mining of cobalt in Europe declined. With the discovery of ore deposits in <color=#3366CC>Ontario</color>, Canada, in 1904 and the discovery
of even larger deposits in the <color=#3366CC>Katanga Province</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Congo</color> in 1914, mining operations shifted again. When the
Shaba conflict started in 1978, the copper mines of Katanga Province nearly stopped production. The impact on the
world cobalt economy from this conflict was smaller than expected: cobalt is a rare metal, the pigment is highly toxic,
and the industry had already established effective ways for recycling cobalt materials. In some cases, industry was able
to change to cobalt-free alternatives.
In 1938, John Livingood and <color=#3366CC>Glenn T. Seaborg</color> discovered the radioisotope <color=#3366CC>cobalt-60</color>. This isotope was famously used
at <color=#3366CC>Columbia University</color> in the 1950s to establish <color=#3366CC>parity</color> violation in radioactive <color=#3366CC>beta decay</color>.
After World War II, the US wanted to guarantee the supply of cobalt ore for military uses (as the Germans had been
doing) and prospected for cobalt within the US. High purity cobalt was highly sought after for its use in jet engines and
gas turbines. An adequate supply of the ore was found in Idaho near Blackbird canyon. Calera Mining Company started
production at the site.
Cobalt demand has further accelerated in the 21st century as an essential constituent of materials used in
rechargeable batteries, superalloys, and catalysts. It has been argued that cobalt will be one of the main objects of
geopolitical competition in a world running on renewable energy and dependent on batteries, but this perspective has
also been criticised for underestimating the power of economic incentives for expanded production.
Occurrence
The stable isotope of cobalt is produced in <color=#3366CC>supernovae</color> through the <color=#3366CC>r-process</color>. It comprises 0.0029% of the Earth's crust
where it is frequently associated with <color=#3366CC>nickel</color>. Both are characteristic components of <color=#3366CC>meteoric iron</color>, though cobalt is much
less abundant in iron meteorites than nickel. As with nickel, cobalt in meteoric iron <color=#3366CC>alloys</color> may have been well enough
protected from oxygen and moisture to remain as the free (but alloyed) metal. In the ocean cobalt typically reacts with
chlorine.
Cobalt in compound form occurs in copper and nickel minerals. It is the major metallic component that combines with
<color=#3366CC>sulfur</color> and arsenic in the sulfidic <color=#3366CC>cobaltite</color> (CoAsS), safflorite (CoAs2), glaucodot ((Co,Fe)AsS), and <color=#3366CC>skutterudite</color>
(CoAs3) minerals. The mineral cattierite is similar to <color=#3366CC>pyrite</color> and occurs together with vaesite in the copper deposits of
<color=#3366CC>Katanga Province</color>. When it reaches the atmosphere, <color=#3366CC>weathering</color> occurs; the sulfide minerals oxidize and form pink
<color=#3366CC>erythrite</color> ("cobalt glance": Co3(AsO4)2*8H2O) and spherocobaltite (CoCO3). Small amounts of cobalt compounds are
found in most rocks, soils, plants, and animals.
Free cobalt (the <color=#3366CC>native metal</color>) was reported from samples in the Kola Superdeep Borehole and in Moon rocks from the
Luna 24 mission, possibly as a result of impacts.
Cobalt is also a constituent of <color=#3366CC>tobacco smoke</color>. The <color=#3366CC>tobacco plant</color> readily absorbs and accumulates <color=#3366CC>heavy metals</color> like
cobalt from the surrounding soil in its leaves. These are subsequently inhaled during <color=#3366CC>tobacco smoking</color>.
Production
The main ores of cobalt are <color=#3366CC>cobaltite</color>, <color=#3366CC>erythrite</color>, glaucodot and <color=#3366CC>skutterudite</color> (see above), but most cobalt is obtained by
reducing the cobalt <color=#3366CC>by-products</color> of nickel and copper mining and <color=#3366CC>smelting</color>.
Since cobalt is generally produced as a by-product, the supply of cobalt depends to a great extent on the economic
feasibility of copper and nickel mining in a given market. Demand for cobalt was projected to grow 6% in 2017.
Primary cobalt deposits are rare, such as those occurring in hydrothermal deposits, associated with ultramafic rocks,
typified by the Bou-Azzer district of <color=#3366CC>Morocco</color>. At such locations, cobalt ores are mined exclusively, albeit at a lower
concentration, and thus require more downstream processing for cobalt extraction.
Several methods exist to separate cobalt from copper and nickel, depending on the concentration of cobalt and the
exact composition of the used ore. One method is froth flotation, in which <color=#3366CC>surfactants</color> bind to ore components, leading
to an enrichment of cobalt ores. Subsequent roasting converts the ores to cobalt sulfate, and the copper and the iron
are oxidized to the oxide. Leaching with water extracts the sulfate together with the arsenates. The residues are further
leached with <color=#3366CC>sulfuric acid</color>, yielding a solution of copper sulfate. Cobalt can also be leached from the slag of copper
smelting.
The products of the above-mentioned processes are transformed into the cobalt oxide (Co3O4). This oxide is reduced
to metal by the aluminothermic reaction or reduction with carbon in a <color=#3366CC>blast furnace</color>.
Extraction
The United States Geological Survey estimates world reserves of cobalt at 11,000,000 metric tons. The <color=#3366CC>Democratic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Republic of the Congo</color> (DRC) currently produces 63% of the world's cobalt. This market share may reach 73% by 2025
if planned expansions by mining producers like <color=#3366CC>Glencore</color> Plc take place as expected. Bloomberg New Energy Finance
has estimated that by 2030, global demand for cobalt could be 47 times more than it was in 2017.
Democratic Republic of the Congo
Changes that Congo made to mining laws in 2002 attracted new investments in Congolese copper and cobalt projects.
In 2005, the top producer of cobalt was the copper deposits in the <color=#3366CC>Democratic Republic of the Congo</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Katanga</color>
<color=#3366CC>Province</color>. Formerly Shaba province, the area had almost 40% of global reserves, reported the British Geological
Survey in 2009.
The Mukondo Mountain project, operated by the Central African Mining and Exploration Company (CAMEC) in Katanga
Province, may be the richest cobalt reserve in the world. It produced an estimated one-third of the total global cobalt
production in 2008. In July 2009, CAMEC announced a long-term agreement to deliver its entire annual <color=#3366CC>production</color> of
cobalt concentrate from Mukondo Mountain to Zhejiang Galico Cobalt & Nickel Materials of China.
In 2016, Chinese ownership of cobalt production in the Congo was estimated at over 10% of global cobalt supply,
forming a key input to the Chinese cobalt refining industry and granting China substantial influence over the global
cobalt supply chain. Chinese control of Congolese cobalt has raised concern in Western nations which have sought to
reduce supply chain reliance upon China and have expressed concern regarding labor and human rights violations in
cobalt mines in the DRC.
Glencore's Mutanda Mine shipped 24,500 tons of cobalt in 2016, 40% of Congo DRC's output and nearly a quarter of
global production. After oversupply, Glencore closed Mutanda for two years in late 2019. Glencore's Katanga Mining
project is resuming as well and should produce 300,000 tons of copper and 20,000 tons of cobalt by 2019, according to
Glencore.
In February 2018, global asset management firm AllianceBernstein defined the DRC as economically "the <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color>
of the electric vehicle age", due to its cobalt resources, as essential to the <color=#3366CC>lithium-ion batteries</color> that drive <color=#3366CC>electric</color>
<color=#3366CC>vehicles</color>.
On 9 March 2018, President <color=#3366CC>Joseph Kabila</color> updated the 2002 mining code, increasing royalty charges and declaring
cobalt and <color=#3366CC>coltan</color> "strategic metals". The 2002 mining code was effectively updated on 4 December 2018.
In February 2025, the DRC implemented a four-month suspension of cobalt exports, citing an oversupply of the metal
amid a price decline to its lowest level in 21 years. Cobalt, a key byproduct of copper mining, is an essential material in
battery technology. The DRC accounts for approximately 75 percent of the global supply. Within the country, the China
Molybdenum Company (CMOC) dominates the industry, contributing roughly 40 percent of the world's cobalt
production. Over the past year, CMOC has significantly increased its output, doubling production from two of its mines
in the DRC from 56,000 tonnes to 114,000 tonnes.
Labor conditions
Artisanal mining supplied 17% to 40% of the DRC production as of 2016. Some 100,000 cobalt miners in Congo DRC
use hand tools to dig hundreds of feet, with little planning and fewer safety measures, say workers and government and
NGO officials, as well as <color=#3366CC>The Washington Post</color> reporters' observations on visits to isolated mines. The lack of safety
precautions frequently causes injuries or death. Mining pollutes the vicinity and exposes local wildlife and indigenous
communities to toxic metals thought to cause birth defects and breathing difficulties, according to health officials.
<color=#3366CC>Child labor</color> is used in mining cobalt from African artisanal mines. Human rights activists have highlighted this and
<color=#3366CC>investigative journalism</color> reporting has confirmed it. This revelation prompted cell phone maker <color=#3366CC>Apple Inc.</color>, on 3 March
2017, to stop buying ore from suppliers such as Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt who source from artisanal mines in the DRC,
and begin using only suppliers that are verified to meet its workplace standards. In 2023, Apple announced it would
convert to using recycled cobalt by 2025 and as of 2026, according to their own press release, all batteries designed by
Apple are made with 100 percent recycled cobalt.
There is a push globally by the <color=#3366CC>EU</color> and major car manufacturers (OEM) for global production of cobalt to be sourced
and –produced sustainably, responsibly and traceability of the supply chain. Mining companies are adopting and
practising ESG initiatives in line with <color=#3366CC>OECD</color> Guidance and putting in place evidence of zero to low carbon footprint
activities in the supply chain production of <color=#3366CC>lithium-ion batteries</color>. These initiatives are already taking place with major
mining companies, artisanal and small-scale mining companies (ASM). Car manufacturers and battery manufacturer
supply chains: Tesla, VW, BMW, BASF and Glencore are participating in several initiatives, such as the Responsible
Cobalt Initiative and Cobalt for Development study. In 2018 BMW Group in partnership with BASF, Samsung SDI and
Samsung Electronics have launched a pilot project in the DRC over one pilot mine, to improve conditions and address
challenges for artisanal miners and the surrounding communities.
The political and ethnic dynamics of the region have in the past caused outbreaks of violence and years of armed
conflict and displaced populations. This instability affected the price of cobalt and also created perverse incentives for
the combatants in the <color=#3366CC>First</color> and <color=#3366CC>Second Congo Wars</color> to prolong the fighting, since access to diamond mines and other
valuable resources helped to finance their military goals—which frequently amounted to genocide—and also enriched
the fighters themselves. While DR Congo has in the 2010s not recently been invaded by neighboring military forces,
some of the richest mineral deposits adjoin areas where Tutsis and Hutus still frequently clash, unrest continues
although on a smaller scale and refugees still flee outbreaks of violence.
Cobalt extracted from small Congolese artisanal mining endeavors in 2007 supplied a single Chinese company, Congo
DongFang International Mining. A subsidiary of Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, one of the world's largest cobalt producers,
Congo DongFang supplied cobalt to some of the world's largest battery manufacturers, who produced batteries for
ubiquitous products like the Apple <color=#3366CC>iPhones</color>. Because of accused labour violations and environmental concerns, LG
Chem subsequently audited Congo DongFang in accordance with OECD guidelines. LG Chem, which also produces
battery materials for car companies, imposed a code of conduct on all suppliers that it inspects.
In December 2019, International Rights Advocates, a human rights NGO, filed a landmark lawsuit against Apple, <color=#3366CC>Tesla</color>,
